entities.summary:
Lê Nhân Tông, the third Emperor of the Lê dynasty, ruled Vietnam from 1453 to 1459. He was born in 1428 in what is now Vietnam and died on November 3, 1459. His reign was marked by power struggles and foreign influence.

Lê Nhân Tông succeeded his father, Lê Thánh Tông, and was just 25 years old when he took the throne. His mother, Queen Dowager Tuyên Từ, played a crucial role in guiding his early decisions.

During his reign, Lê Nhân Tông faced significant challenges from neighboring kingdoms, including the Ming dynasty in China and the Cham kingdom in modern-day Vietnam. He also struggled to maintain the power and influence of the Lê dynasty, which had been founded by his great-grandfather, Lê Lợi.

Despite these challenges, Lê Nhân Tông implemented several key policies to strengthen the dynasty, including the promotion of trade and commerce. He also oversaw the construction of several important infrastructure projects, including roads, bridges, and canals.

However, Lê Nhân Tông's reign was ultimately cut short when he was murdered in a coup led by his half-brother, Lê Lợi. His death marked the end of the Lê dynasty's dominance in Vietnam and paved the way for the Nguyen dynasty's rise to power.

The legacy of Lê Nhân Tông continues to be felt in Vietnam today, where he is remembered as a symbol of the nation's rich history and cultural heritage. His story has also inspired numerous works of literature, art, and music, cementing his place in Vietnamese folklore.

Lê Nhân Tông, the third Emperor of the Lê dynasty, ruled Vietnam from 1453 to 1459. Born as Lê Bang Cơ in 1441, he was a grandson of the dynasty's founder Lê Lợi and ascended to the throne at a young age. His reign was marked by power struggles and internal conflicts, with his mother, Queen Dowager Tuyên Từ, holding significant influence.

Despite these challenges, Lê Nhân Tông oversaw the expansion of the Lê dynasty's territories and the development of its administrative systems. He also promoted the arts and culture, with many notable works of literature and architecture emerging during his reign.

However, his reign came to an end in 1459, when he was murdered in a coup led by his half-brother, Lê Nhân Tông's cousin, Lê Nghiêu.

Lê Nhân Tông's legacy is complex and multifaceted, reflecting both the strengths and weaknesses of the Lê dynasty during this period.

This emperor's life and reign serve as a reminder of the intricate web of power, politics, and culture that defined medieval Vietnam.
